data.title: IFA Berlin Recap Part 2: More Diverse Sustainability Approaches
data.description:
Earlier this week, IFA Berlin wrapped up. If there was a consistent theme around clean technology, it was that sustainability is not just one thing, but a diverse range of approaches.

Some of the innovations that we focus on in the US have become routine in Germany. Although I had not been to IFA before, I got the sense that sustainability was not as prevalent in messaging as it was in the past. Heat pumps seemed to be the norm. Induction cooktops greatly outnumbered gas or resistance. Energy efficiency tended to be an expectation more than a differentiator to highlight.

However, clean technology still seems to have a strong appeal in Europe. That showed up in diverse ways through multiple products, some of which are highlighted here.

Bosch showed off their Green Collection, with up to 50% less CO2 from production materials. Although we have tended to focus on efficiency, appliances are heavy and contain a large amount of material. The matte black finish also looked sleek and a bit different than typical kitchen appliances.

Ferre dedicated space to the sustainability of their packaging, made from recycled materials.

Gorenje had one of the largest displays dedicated to sustainability, with efforts extending from sourcing, materials and manufacturing to energy efficiency and packaging. The company makes a range of efficient appliances in their factory in Slovenia, as the fourth largest appliance manufacturer in Europe. In talking with one of their product people, they said that one of the main ways that they foster sustainability is by improving the performance of electrified options, including high-output induction cooktops and electric pizza ovens. While many in the US are not familiar with Gorenje, they are part of Hisense, and also manufacture for several other brands. If you buy an appliance made in Slovenia, there is a good chance that it was made by Gorenje.

Midea highlighted the switch to R290 refrigerant (propane) for their heat pumps, which is far more environmentally friendly than many traditional refrigerants. However, while they gave it the most attention, they were not alone. Europe appears to be transitioning to R290 rapidly.

Chigo/iCongo also showed off their R290 air conditioners, with sustainability-focused messaging. The brand claims 30% energy savings thanks to “AI-powered dynamic adjustments.” That is an impressive claimed efficiency improvement that I would like to see further test results to support.

While heat pumps were dominant, Eurom displayed their infrared home heaters. While not as efficient as heat pumps on a per-BTU basis, these heaters can invisibly radiate long-wavelength infrared onto the surfaces where it is needed. Like how the sun warms the earth. For example, the heaters could be focused on a seating area in an open concept living room, providing a level of comfort while not having to heat all the air in the entire room or entire home. As such, an entire home could be kept at a lower overall temperature, while the areas with occupants could be heated with infrared. Integrating sensors and intelligence could extend the concept. It was an interesting idea that has some potential.

Moving on to materials, REEDEE displayed recycled TPU and PET plastic films to be used as screen protectors. While many people put plastics into recycling bins, they often end up in the landfill or are burned anyway. Providing paths to recycle plastics reduces both pollution and the amount of plastic needed in the first place.

 

Gforest, or Ningbo Green Forest Electronic Technology, manufactures a range of products, often for white label. They had their food recyclers on display, which break down and dry food to be used in a garden, utilizing a high-efficiency heater. In addition, they showed off mister fans that use a fine spray of water to cool evaporatively. While not an outright replacement for air conditioning, they can provide needed relief when it is not available. Especially in many European homes, where air conditioning is not common, but periods of extreme heat are increasing in prevalence and intensity. One current model places a fan on top of a water tank. However, they also showed off a prototype that adds misting capability to an adhesive puck that can mount to the center of an existing fan case, with a water tank that attaches to the central pole. It is a simple idea, but people would not need to buy a new fan, and they could put off investing in energy-intensive air conditioning a little longer. Not all clean technology needs to be complicated.

Beyond the new technology, there was also some attention to repairing existing electronics. Repartly offered parts and repair of electronics and appliances, available within Germany. This can make repairs faster and more affordable, while reducing shipping costs and emissions. Although you likely would not want to keep an inefficient model for an extended time, by repairing electronics, rather than throwing them away, the embodied energy needed for manufacturing is reduced, while waste management becomes less of a challenge.

In terms of EVs, beyond XPENG and Xiaomi, Volkswagen had their new ID.Polo and ID.Cross on display. The ID.Polo model gets back to their design roots and looked attractive, if not groundbreaking. While the ID.Cross enters the fiercely competitive crossover segment, the smaller ID.Polo could prove to be popular on the tight roads of Europe. If you needed something even smaller, Volkswagen also licensed their brand to an e-bike available for test rides.

Overall, even in markets where sustainability isn’t the primary focus, there are many ways it can be integrated into products and services. From major brands to regional manufacturers. From material suppliers to repair and recycling. There isn’t one silver bullet that will provide a single simple solution to all our challenges. However, the diversity of approaches also creates a diversity of ways to make an impact. IFA, which stands for Innovation For All, demonstrates that all of us have an opportunity to engage with sustainable innovations, through our businesses, our purchases and how we live our lives.

The Electric Vehicles Leading Their Categories in California
data.description:
Electric vehicles have seen a real drop-off of sales across the US this year, including in California, the main EV market in the country by far. Whereas in previous quarters and years electric vehicle models were peppered across the top 5 of numerous vehicle categories — even topping a few of them — the story has gotten a bit drab this year. A handful of vehicle categories that had EVs in their top 5 no longer do. That said, more than a half-dozen categories do still have EVs in their top five. Let’s have a look. (Note that static versions of the images embedded below are also included at the bottom of this article.)

First of all, the Tesla Model Y’s sales may have dropped, but they are still several times higher than the sales of other luxury compact SUVs.

Similarly, the Tesla Model 3 has continued crushing other models in the “near luxury” vehicle class. No other model comes close, with the Model 3 scoring almost four times more

The Tesla Model X keeps the party going for the Tesla brand. Even in the midst of being discontinued, the Model was the 5th best selling model in its category.

The Ford Mustang Mach-E didn’t get as many sales as the Model X, but it did come in 4th in its category, a very competitive one.

The Rivian R1S was right behind the Ford Mustang Mach-E in volume terms, but it was in 2nd place in its own category — not too shabby.

Again, despite being phased out, the Tesla Model S performed well in its vehicle class, coming in 2nd place among all luxury and high-end sports cars. So, Tesla placed almost all of its vehicles in the top five of their vehicle categories. (I was thinking Tesla got all of them in, but then remembered about the Cybertruck.)

Last (and least), the Volkswagen ID. Buzz seems to have barely slipped into the top five of the minivan category — but how many minivans are on the market in the first place?

At the end of it all, the Tesla Model Y was the best selling model in the Golden State by far, the Tesla Model 3 was in 9th, and no other EV models were in the top 10. The Tesla Model Y crushed all other SUVs or trucks of any price or size, and the Tesla Model 3 came in 4th among all cars.

Anything else jump out to you?

data.title: Aberdeen Paid £556k Per Hydrogen Bus. Five Years Later, First Bus Is Paying £30k
data.description:
Aberdeen’s hydrogen double-deckers have finally produced a useful market price, and it is more revealing than another theoretical argument about fuel-cell efficiency, hydrogen costs or refuelling infrastructure. First Bus is set to buy 23 Wrightbus StreetDeck Hydroliners for £30,000 each. Aberdeen City Council originally spent about £13.9 million on the 25-bus fleet, an average of roughly £556,000 per vehicle, which means the commercial operator taking almost the entire fleet is paying just 5.4% of the original average acquisition cost. These are not elderly buses being disposed of after 15 years of service. They entered service in 2021 and accumulated only about three and a half years of revenue operation before hydrogen-supply problems left them parked.

The number matters because Aberdeen actually tested the market rather than simply estimating residual value on a spreadsheet. The confidential council briefing obtained by the Press and Journal says Aberdeen received four other bids after approaching the market, including proposals to take buses for free and another offering £1 per vehicle. First’s £30,000 therefore should not be interpreted merely as an unusually aggressive negotiation by a sophisticated buyer. The city went looking for purchasers and discovered what organizations were prepared to pay for relatively young specialist zero-emission vehicles whose original drivetrain no longer had much obvious commercial appeal. When Aberdeen first announced that it wanted to dispose of the fleet, I argued that there was no deep or liquid secondary market for used hydrogen buses. We now have a real transaction against which that proposition can be tested.

This is the short version of a deeper TFIE Strategy Briefing analysis that tests what the £30,000 price actually means once normal fleet depreciation, the value of the underlying bus and the economics of removing the hydrogen system are put on the same basis. The sale price is the first verdict. What First Bus does next is the more interesting one.

What First is buying is equally important. It does not appear to be buying 23 hydrogen buses because it wants to expand hydrogen operations. The council briefing says First is drawing up plans to overhaul them for battery-electric use. That is technically plausible, but it is not simply a matter of replacing one box with another. A fuel-cell bus already has electric traction, yet a useful battery conversion still means removing the hydrogen storage and fuel-cell system, finding space and structural capacity for several hundred kilowatt-hours of batteries, managing weight distribution and axle loads, integrating charging and thermal management, adapting controls and auxiliaries, and certifying and warranting the resulting vehicle. The £30,000 acquisition price is therefore only the opening number in a much larger decision about how much additional capital these vehicles deserve.

First is about as well positioned as any operator could be to investigate that decision. It has operated the Hydroliners since new, so it knows their maintenance histories and operating condition. It has also already made a substantial commitment to battery-electric operation in Aberdeen: its £12.7 million investment in 36 electric buses included 24 new Wrightbus battery-electric double-deckers and 12 existing buses repowered from internal combustion to battery electric. Its King Street depot has rapid DC charging infrastructure, and First was the first UK operator to order conversions from Wrightbus’s NewPower business after helping develop the programme with two trial vehicles. This is not a buyer encountering bus repowering for the first time.

Yet First has not publicly committed to converting all 23 former hydrogen buses. The council briefing says it is developing plans for electric conversion, but there is no disclosed battery capacity, conversion supplier, final engineering configuration, cost per vehicle, warranty package or return-to-service schedule. The vehicle transfers themselves are staged, with seven expected before the end of March 2027 and the remaining 16 during financial year 2027–28. There is no public evidence of a contractual walk-away option, so this should not be described as a formal conversion trial. Economically, however, First has limited its exposure very effectively. Buying a known five-year-old StreetDeck chassis and body for £30,000 is cheap. Committing serious capital to turn it into a reliable battery-electric bus is a separate decision.

That distinction is why the Aberdeen case deserves attention beyond one Scottish fleet. Public clean-transport programmes routinely compare acquisition costs, grants, fuel expenses, operating emissions and infrastructure requirements, but residual value and exit optionality receive much less attention. A technology can work in service and still destroy capital if it creates an asset that few buyers want when the original operating model breaks down. Aberdeen has already absorbed almost all of that capital loss, leaving First with extremely inexpensive donor vehicles and enough economic headroom to investigate a conversion that would look very different if it first had to pay a normal used-bus price.

There are two useful ways the next stage can go. If First develops a reliable and economical conversion package, Aberdeen will show that at least some stranded hydrogen buses can be salvaged under unusually favourable conditions: relatively young vehicles bought for almost nothing, acquired by the operator that has known them since new, based on a familiar platform and supported by existing battery-bus expertise and charging infrastructure. That would be a useful result, but it would not demonstrate that hydrogen buses retained substantial resale value. Much of the useful value would instead have been recovered by removing the equipment that made them hydrogen buses.

If First cannot make the conversion economics work under those conditions, the conclusion becomes much less comfortable for other stranded hydrogen fleets. Few are likely to combine such a low donor-vehicle price with such young buses, an experienced incumbent operator, existing charging, a familiar chassis and an established repowering relationship. Aberdeen has already received one answer from the used-vehicle market: a bus that cost roughly £556,000 five years ago is worth £30,000 to the commercial operator taking almost the entire fleet. The more interesting question now is how much First decides those buses are worth after the hydrogen equipment comes out.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing analysis works through the residual-value reference class, conversion economics and what either outcome would mean for other stranded hydrogen fleets.

data.title: Volkswagen & Skoda Eye Investments In India
data.description:
Twenty or more years ago, automakers in the US and Europe turned their covetous eyes toward China, the most populous nation on Earth. As that country sought to drag itself up from the turmoil of the Cultural Revolution and become a modern economic powerhouse, the prospect of selling automobiles to China’s burgeoning middle class was too enticing to ignore. For years, the profits for selling cars in China gave a much needed boost to corporate balance sheets in Detroit, Munich, Stuttgart, and Wolfsburg.

Although we are seldom aware of it, change is happening all around us all the time. While all eyes have been fixed on China, India is now the most populous nation in the world. Chinese customers are opting more often for domestic nameplates, which has ended the gravy train for the likes of GM, BMW, Mercedes, and Volkswagen.

But could lightning strike twice for those foreign manufacturers? Volkswagen in particular is poised for disruptive changes, as it is now building more cars in Germany than it can sell. Could it learn from the experience of the Chinese and create a new source of revenue by selling its cars in other countries?

Volkswagen Looks Toward India

That possibility is being actively explored by both Volkswagen and Skoda, which are both seeking new manufacturing opportunities in India. According to a report by Germany’s Handelsblatt, the companies have entered into a memorandum of understanding with Indian conglomerate JSW. While it is just a preliminary agreement, it contains the rather extraordinary stipulation that JSW would control 51 percent of the joint venture, with Volkswagen controlling only 49 percent.

Klaus Zellmer, the CEO of Skoda, describes the MOU as an expression of intent “to explore the fundamental principles of a strategic partnership. The planned collaboration aims to enhance competitiveness through an expanded product portfolio, greater localisation, and the expansion of production and development capabilities.” He said in a recent interview, “I am convinced that we can do better with an Indian partner.” The planned collaboration with JSW is expected to benefit from “local roots, local networks and cultural connections, in order to know what is really right and important in India.”

For context, the standard joint venture agreement that propelled many US and European companies to success has been 50/50 for decades. One might argue that such a small change should have little practical effect, but in practice it changes everything. The minority partner can suggest, plead, wheedle, and cajole, but, in the end, the majority partner makes all the decisions.

Volkswagen has been trying to establish a presence in India for many years. It first entered the market in India in 2001, using its Skoda brand to lead the way. Then, in 2007, Volkswagen followed with its own cars. Over the years, it has partnered with Suzuki, Tata, and Mahindra — all to no avail.

Klaus Zellmer Sees An Opening

Skoda has recently exited the Chinese market, and Zellmer thinks India is the country his company should transition to next. “The Indian market today is as dynamic as the Chinese market was a few years ago. We have two plants in India, an established dealer network, and very good quality. With just under three per cent market share, we are a relatively small player, but Sloda is still the most successful European brand in India. This is a solid foundation to build on.”

Skoda doubled its sales in India in 2025, recording the highest year-on-year growth rate in any of the markets where its vehicles are sold. Together, VW and Skoda increased their sales in India by 36 percent to 117,000 — all gasoline powered vehicles like the Kylak pictured above.

Politics plays a role here as well. China and India share a more than 2000 mile long border and have engaged in numerous military skirmishes over the years. While the tensions between the two have stabilized of late, India is in no hurry to let in a slew of Chinese imports. As a result, Chinese automakers have struggled to invest in India, which Zelmer sees as an opportunity for Skoda.

The JSW partnership could be the key to VW and Skoda plans to sell electric cars in India. According to the Indian magazine Autocar Professional, JSW — if the MOU is finalized — could finance products based on Volkswagen’s planned India Main Platform, which is a derivation of its China Main Platform. The timetable for Volkswagen to offer electric cars in India is currently 2028.

The JSW conglomerate, which includes the steel producer JSW Steel, is already active in the automotive business. In 2023, the group founded the joint venture JSW MG Motor India together with the Chinese manufacturer SAIC. Under the name JSW Motors, the conglomerate also plans to establish its own electric car brand, utilizing the technology of the Chinese manufacturer Chery. JSW has not yet commented on the planned partnership with Volkswagen.

Third Largest New Car Market

India is the world’s third-largest car market in terms of sales figures. In the last fiscal year, which ended in March, 4.6 million passenger cars were sold in the country — eight percent more than in the previous year. Only China and the USA sell more cars. Although, 4.6 million cars in a nation of 1.48 billion people is a mere pittance. India lacks much of the transportation and charging infrastructure that China has built in the past several decades and has been noncommittal about incentive programs that encourage people to purchase electric cars.

In other words, the new car market in India is not China 2.0. Volkswagen Group is desperate for financial windfall to replace its profits from China — profits which now have largely evaporated. It has tried to crack the Indian market in the past and gotten nowhere. Will this time be different? Klaus Zellmer and Oliver Blume certainly hope so.

data.title: Tesla Superchargers For Non-Tesla EVs On The Mass Pike!
data.description:
I was wedged between tractor trailers as I held to the extreme right hand lane. Vehicles entered from frequent on-ramps and forced me to make quick lane changes to the left. Road construction narrowed lanes and forced me to merge into oncoming traffic.

I veered in and out, around vehicles of varying speed. Hubby and I were traveling home on a series of New England highways from our August vacation in Maine. In retrospect, I had overestimated the range that our 2017 Chevy Bolt was actually capable of producing on a highway, and I was attempting to maintain the lowest possible speed while not becoming an obstacle for other vehicles around me.

At our summer home, hubby and I plug the Bolt into an everyday wall outlet and let it do its thing — usually providing us with around 250 projected miles at 80% charge overnight. That’s fabulous for our day trips — we almost always get where we’re going as we cruise around New England in the summer.

Sure, the Bolt has good overall range in comparison to other non-Tesla EVs.

But highways? Uh uh.

For this longer road trip, on the way north we charged at a Kittery, Maine Tesla Supercharger that was also configured for non-Tesla EVs. We had purchased the NACS adapter last summer and found it very handy to have on hand.

Like all EVs, the Bolt loves low and slow roads. At our destination of Ogunquit and surrounding area, the roads embrace the granite coast and meander in and out of switchbacks, with lots of 25 mph signage warnings. If the GPS alternatively suggests Route 1, well, the traffic there in the summer is thick, so average travel speeds stay low.

Sometimes we charge the Bolt at our vacation accommodation as we travel, but this site overlooking the Atlantic Ocean didn’t offer any EV charging. It was such a special place that we didn’t care. We would make other charging arrangements.

Starting out for home with 200 miles of projected range, it seemed as if we would get back to Connecticut with just enough miles to spare any range anxiety.

Nope.

Getting on I-95 heading south changed the narrative quickly. The traffic whizzed along well above the posted speed limit. So I needed to adjust my speed to at least 68 mph minimally once I was caught up in the highway activity flurry. The Bolt’s calculated distance to home of 138 miles home didn’t begin to correlate with the original 200 mile range on the guess-o-meter. Falling, falling.

Before you admonish me, allow me to note that, I definitely had researched fast chargers along the route home. Using the Tesla app on my iPhone (our other car is a Model Y, which is happily garaged right now in Florida), I had swiped through to the “Charge Your Other EV” link in order to find chargers that accommodated non-Tesla EVs.

But, just ’cause you find a Tesla Supercharger, it doesn’t mean you’re golden. Take it from me: don’t try to search for Tesla Superchargers on your laptop using Google Maps, for example. I’ve done it and won’t ever do it again. Every single Supercharger appears, but not all are compatible with a non-Tesla EV. It can lead to marital disputes to target a fast charger that doesn’t exist!

Anyway, yes, there were opportunities to charge midway to Connecticut, but most were well off the highway in a swirl of congested old factory cities and multiple roads.

I identified the Charlton westbound rest area as available with the NACS adapter, and it was at the three-quarter mark of our trip. Those criteria checked off important boxes, but I was still uncertain. It was only last year that I tried to stop at the Charlton Westbound rest area off the Mass Turnpike but found that the NACS adapters weren’t accepted.

Had something changed for 2026? Was it a tech error? Would I arrive again at Charlton, only to find that I was out of luck, with an inadequate 46 miles left of projected range to get home?

Hubby and I made a pact that, if the Charlton Westbound rest area would not take non-Tesla EVs as advertised, we’d have to crawl on back roads to an available charger and get at least 20 more miles to make it home.

I pulled into the Charlton rest area and located the shining red-and-white Tesla Superchargers at the back of the parking lot. All the vehicles currently charging were Teslas. Fingers crossed, I parked. Hubby pulled out the NACS adapter. I engaged the Tesla app to the correct charging station. We both waited to see if the Bolt’s green light would start flashing to confirm it had made a connection with the Tesla Supercharger mothership.

The NACS adapter worked! It was such a relief. We gladly sat for an hour to charge to 80%.

Once upon a time, I followed a wonderful professor from the University of New Hampshire. To paraphrase Donald Murray, once you learn a new idea, the world bombards you with information about it.

The Boston Globe this morning explained why the Charlton Westbound Tesla Superchargers now accept non-Tesla EVs.

In summary, just a week ago, Tesla, under an amended agreement with the Massachusetts Department of Transportation, opened its fast charging stations at state-owned rest stops on the Mass Pike and I-95 to other brands of electric vehicles. The agreement came after MassDOT failed to improve major transit charging options after convenience store operator Applegreen didn’t come through to overhaul 17 state rest stops and provide new fast charging.

So now there are 32 fast charging ports on the major Massachusetts highways, which doubles the number of ports open to all EV drivers at state-owned rest stops.

Whew. The timing was ideal for me and the other non-Tesla EVs that were soon buzzing in and out of the Charlton Westbound rest area. If you build it, they will follow.

data.title: Lynk & Co Chooses Volvo Cars As Exclusive European Distributor
data.description:
Lynk & Co is one of those 100% plugin vehicle brands sitting under the giant Geely umbrella. It has had its ups and downs, and it’s not blazing a rapid, insane path of growth like a few other Chinese EV startups, but it’s doing alright. A key focus of the brand is the European market, and it’s looking to achieve much more there via a new partnership.

Yes, as you can see in the title, that partnership is with Volvo Cars (another company under the Geely umbrella). Starting in January 2027, Volvo Cars will be Lynk & Co’s exclusive distributor in Europe.

“The agreement marks an important milestone in Lynk & Co’s European journey and creates a strong foundation for the brand’s continued growth across the region. By leveraging Volvo Cars’ established commercial infrastructure, retail network and service footprint, Lynk & Co will be able to reach more customers, strengthen its market presence and further improve access to its products and services.”

It will certainly help to get Lynk & Co’s cars out to a lot more locations, and also promise service at established, trusted dealerships. This finally gives Lynk & Co a big runway to try to launch from. Also, given that Volvo is originally a European (Swedish) company that many Europeans love and trust, exclusively putting Lynk & Co electric vehicles in its dealerships basically makes Lynk & Co look like another luxury brand of Volvo. Will it work to jack up Lynk & Co sales? Maybe — but it’s better than what the company has been doing. It gives the brand a better chance.

“Europe remains a strategically important market for Lynk & Co, and the new distribution model is designed to support the brand’s next phase of growth while enhancing the customer experience across the region,” Lynk & Co says.

“This partnership brings together Volvo Cars’ established commercial infrastructure and Lynk & Co’s distinctive brand and product proposition, says Mo Wang, CEO of Lynk & Co International. Our focus will be to ensure strong strategic alignment between Europe and our global organization, preserve the distinctiveness of the Lynk & Co brand and work closely with Volvo Cars to turn this partnership into sustainable long-term growth,” Mo Wang, CEO of Lynk & Co International, adds.

“Today’s announcement represents an exciting new chapter for Lynk & Co in Europe, said Martin Persson, Head of Lynk & Co Europe at Volvo Cars. Over the past years, Lynk & Co has successfully expanded to 25 European markets and built a network of more than 140 partner-operated sales points, leveraging the collaboration with Volvo Cars retailers. With Volvo Cars now becoming the exclusive distributor for Lynk & Co in Europe, we are confident that we can take that growth to the next level. By combining Lynk & Co’s distinctive brand and product portfolio, the strength and innovation capabilities of Geely Auto Group, and Volvo Cars’ proven commercial operations and market reach, we are creating a strong foundation for sustainable long-term growth. Together, we see significant opportunities to further strengthen Lynk & Co’s position in Europe and establish the brand as an increasingly relevant player in the evolving automotive landscape,” says Martin Persson, Head of Lynk & Co Europe at Volvo Cars.

The arguments are clear. The idea seems good. But e’ll see how it works. Any thoughts?

data.title: China Aims For 70% Plugin Vehicle Sales By 2030 — Hit 61% In August
data.description:
China has just released its newest 5-year development plan for plugin vehicles — its 15th — and the plan includes a target of reaching 70% plugin vehicle (or “new energy vehicle”) sales by 2030. That sounds pretty good — certainly much better than the US will do, and probably better than Europe will do. However, when you look at where the market is already, one has to think that it’s not super ambitious and the country might do much better.

Just to clarify, this 70% plugin vehicle share target is for passenger vehicle sales. The target for commercial vehicle sales is 40% plugin vehicle share. The thing is: the market was already at 61% (60.6%) last month. With that being the case, how much more needs to change to get to 70%, and how much will actually change in the industry and market by then?

Of course, as we’ve seen, several Chinese EV producers are keen to grow their sales well beyond what they can achieve even in China, so are targeting more and more sales abroad as well. That’s not the focus of this 5-year plan, but adding those ambitious targets onto the country’s targets, some of those automakers are looking to achieve huge EV sales numbers.

Naturally, as is the trend lately, a strong focus was also put on autonomous driving in the 5-year plan.

Beyond superficial targets and basically simple forecasts, though, the 5-year plan also gets into some complicated, difficult topics and the nitty gritty of the growing the industry sustainably. “Alongside broader adoption, the plan explicitly calls for stronger capacity monitoring and controls, strict conditions for projects establishing new standalone NEV manufacturers, and tighter management of battery production capacity,” CnEVPost writes. “China will step up mergers, restructuring and cross-regional consolidation among automakers, using market-based and legal mechanisms to phase out outdated and inefficient capacity and improve overall utilization.

“Oversight of market competition is another priority. The plan calls for stronger antitrust, unfair competition and pricing enforcement, as well as curbs on improper local efforts to attract investment through unauthorized subsidies, tax breaks and preferential land policies.

“The document also calls for better oversight of industry data disclosures and corporate payments, action against improper market intervention, and faster development of a unified national market.”

Sounds smart. If only every country was as logical, sensible, and intelligent.

Along with the above, there were also key parts focused on:

  • automotive chips
  • critical basic materials
  • operating systems
  • industrial software
  • battery safety
  • charging rates
  • low-temperature performance
  • AI
  • smart homes and robots
  • vehicle efficiency
  • V2G
  • heavy-duty electric trucks
  • and labor productivity.

Again, can we get some of that logical foresight, common sense, and vision over here in the United States?
